title: A Full 3D Portrait of a Molecule's Wavefunction
hook: The wavefunction is quantum mechanics' most fundamental object and its most elusive one. A Göttingen team has now reconstructed one in three dimensions for a real molecule.
key_points: A wavefunction encodes everything knowable about a quantum system, but it is not something you can point a camera at.
Earlier orbital imaging captured flat projections; this work reconstructs the full three-dimensional shape.
The method combines photoelectron measurements with newly designed reconstruction algorithms.
The target was a nanometre-sized organic molecule, whose molecular orbital was mapped in detail.
Reported resolution beats the spacing between the molecule's own carbon atoms.
content_html: Quantum mechanics says everything knowable about a molecule's electrons lives in its wavefunction — yet the wavefunction itself is famously hard to get at. You cannot photograph a probability amplitude; you can only infer it from what measurements come out. Researchers at the University of Göttingen report they have reconstructed one in full three dimensions for a real, nanometre-sized organic molecule.
extra_html: The team combined advanced photoelectron measurements — knocking electrons out of the molecule and recording where they land — with newly designed reconstruction algorithms that turn those distributions back into the orbital they came from. Earlier orbital-imaging work generally produced flat projections; per the group's account, this reconstruction is three-dimensional and resolves detail finer than the spacing between the molecule's own carbon atoms. Getting a direct handle on orbital shape matters because orbitals govern how molecules bond, absorb light, and react.

related.title: What Makes Quantum Physics Weird
related.hook: In the quantum world energy comes in lumps, particles act like waves, and you can't pin down everything at once — and yet it's our best-tested theory.

related.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
related.hook: Nature sets a hard limit: the more precisely you know where a particle is, the less you can know about how it's moving. It's not sloppy measurement — it's built into reality.

related.title: The Quantum Theory Where Particles Have Positions
related.hook: Pilot-wave theory takes the radical step of saying particles always have definite positions, guided by the wave function. It reproduces all of quantum mechanics — at a price.

related.title: Inside the Atom
related.hook: An atom is almost entirely empty space wrapped around a tiny, dense nucleus — and the number of protons in that nucleus is what makes an atom gold instead of oxygen.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a wavefunction hard to observe directly?
flashcards.back_html: It is not a physical object sitting in space — it encodes the probabilities of measurement outcomes, so it has to be reconstructed from many measurements rather than photographed.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Göttingen team measure to reconstruct the molecular orbital?

choices.text: Photoelectrons emitted from the molecule, fed into new reconstruction algorithms
Neutrons scattered off the molecule's nuclei

flashcards.explanation_html: Advanced photoelectron measurements plus purpose-built algorithms let them build a complete 3D image of the orbital.

flashcards.prompt: What makes this reconstruction notable compared with earlier orbital imaging?
flashcards.back_html: It is a complete 3D image rather than a flat projection, and it resolves features smaller than the spacing between the molecule's carbon atoms.
